title: Finishing pigs for slaughter weight
subtitle: A bacon pig at 85 kg liveweight is not the same animal as a pork pig at 65 kg. Target the right weight for what you want out of the carcass.
excerpt: Slaughter weight determines the cut sizes, fat depth, and yield of the finished carcass. A pig slaughtered too light gives small joints and no back fat for bacon curing. Too heavy and the fat depth climbs faster than the meat. Here is how to match target liveweight to the product, manage the finishing feed, and time the abattoir booking.
sourceNotes: AHDB Pork, managing deadweight and carcass quality in pigs. Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (1994), home pig production chapter. John Seymour, The New Complete Book of Self-Sufficiency (2003), pig to pork chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: The weight of the carcass after slaughter, once the head, feet, offal, and skin have been removed. Typically 72–76% of liveweight for pigs.
The industry standard measurement of subcutaneous fat taken 65 mm from the spine at the last rib. A P2 reading below 12 mm indicates a lean carcass; above 16 mm indicates excess fat.

content.text: The right slaughter weight depends on what you are making. A

of 55-65 kg yields pork-weight joints, smaller, leaner, better suited to roasting whole or cutting into pork steaks and chops. A deadweight of 65-75 kg gives bacon-weight carcasses with enough fat depth for long-cure bacon and meaningful back joints. Above 75 kg deadweight you are in heavy pig territory, suitable for charcuterie and for the fat-rich cuts used in sausage making.
Pork (fresh joints, small cuts): 65-75 kg liveweight. Deadweight around 50 kg.
Bacon: 80-95 kg liveweight. P2 fat depth of 10-14 mm on the carcass.
Heavy pork for charcuterie: 100-130 kg liveweight. Higher fat depth gives the intramuscular fat traditional cured meats depend on.
Suckling pig (whole roast): 15-25 kg liveweight, slaughtered young. Rare for smallholders, a different management track.

Switch from grower to finishing ration when the pig reaches 50-55 kg. Finishing feed has lower protein and higher energy to deposit fat rather than lean tissue. Feed at around 2.5% of liveweight per day in two meals, and track body condition fortnightly. A pig building
too fast, visible rounding at the shoulders and hindquarters, can have its ration cut by 10-15% rather than the diet changed.

Estimate the remaining weeks to target weight from current weight. A well-fed finisher adds 0.5-0.7 kg liveweight per day. If the pig is currently at 65 kg and the target is 85 kg, it needs around 30 more days. Book the abattoir slot with a 2-3 week buffer from your estimate: early slots can be filled if the pig is ahead of schedule, late slots used if growth slows.

Under the Animal By-Products Regulations, pigs must be slaughtered at a licensed abattoir for the meat to enter the food chain or be given to others. Home slaughter for your own consumption is permitted in law but requires a competent operator and is not discussed here.

All pig movements require an eAML2 (electronic Animal Movement Licence) submitted online through the APHA website before the animals leave the holding. This applies to movements to an abattoir. The receiving abattoir's CPH number goes in the destination field. The movement document number must accompany the animals.
